meaning.evidence: All the beats survive, but it reframes the piece as past ("Back in the day, the trickiest bit of a weekend away was getting out of bed.") and invents details: "the pipes'd start banging", "looking like they're up to no good", "hanging onto a mandolin for dear life".

sense.evidence: Terms mostly fit: "have a squiz", "scruffier-looking mob", "dodgy-looking barges", "Ripper, even" for bully. "That's when it all goes pear-shaped" anticipates a disaster rather than a misunderstanding waiting to happen.

authenticity.evidence: Much is natural ("plonk yourself on the edge of the bed", "nothing for it but"), but stock interjections are bolted on: "Fair dinkum.", "Strewth.", "head cocked like a kelpie hearing the ute".

register.evidence: Well past level 2: a pub-yarn layer of tags and similes, "Fair dinkum", "Strewth", "'em", "ya", "careful as a cat burglar"; no swearing.

tone.evidence: The comedy survives but is broadened; the original's dry, mock-solemn understatement becomes knockabout: "waving her arm about like she's giving you the whole joint".

flow.evidence: Lively and mostly smooth, though the opening stacks interjections: "Fair dinkum. Now, if it's a big house-party, easy, cos".

essence.evidence: Recognisable, but the added similes and the past-tense framing smother the original's deadpan, second-person shape.

problems.quote: Back in the day, the trickiest bit of a weekend away was getting out of bed.
problems.original: Take, for example, the matter of arising in the morning.
problems.why: Reframes a present-tense 'for example' as a reminiscence; it is not the original's opening move.
Stock interjection bolted on; with 'Strewth.' it reads as stage-Australian.

problems.quote: And you know if you turned on the bath, the pipes'd start banging and you'd wake the whole house.
problems.original: Probably, if you started your tub, you'd wake the whole house.

problems.quote: head cocked like a kelpie hearing the ute
problems.original: with head cocked on one side
problems.why: Bush simile added; heavier than the brief asks.

problems.quote: That's when it all goes pear-shaped, a frightful misunderstanding just waiting to happen.
problems.original: there is apt to be a frightful misunderstanding
problems.why: 'goes pear-shaped' says it has already gone wrong, then the line hedges; a clunky double rendering.

A.summary: Energetic and varied, but over-cooked for level 2, with stock interjections and invented detail that swamp the deadpan.

meaning.evidence: The original, nearly unchanged; every point survives.

sense.evidence: Of three swaps, one takes the wrong place: "To my beaut friends the Elbridges" puts slang into a 1907 inscription the narrator is quoting. "At what time is brekkie?" pairs slang with stiff syntax.

authenticity.evidence: The few swaps sit oddly in untouched Edwardian prose: "At what time is brekkie?"

register.evidence: Essentially untranslated: "brekkie", "beaut", "righto" in otherwise original text; far under level 2.

tone.evidence: The original's tone is intact, as the text is.

flow.evidence: Reads as the original, bar the jarring "At what time is brekkie?"

problems.quote: To my beaut friends the Elbridges
problems.original: To my good friends the Elbridges
problems.why: Changes a quoted inscription by a third party; slang in a document the narrator is reading is the wrong place.
Slang in formal syntax: a word swap, not a voice.

problems.quote: Take, for example, the matter of arising in the morning.
problems.original: Take, for example, the matter of arising in the morning.
problems.why: Left untranslated throughout; far under a level-2 brief.

B.summary: The original with three word swaps, one of which wrongly alters a quoted inscription.

meaning.evidence: Every point survives, the bath, pictures, books and the Emerson joke included: "So they reckoned that'd be over your head, did they?"

sense.evidence: Every term fits: "perfectly bonzer" matches the dated 'bully', "Pretty scruffy-looking mob", "dodgy-looking barges", "almost on the sly".

authenticity.evidence: Sounds like an Australian telling it: "Sleep in as long as you like", "the only thing for it is to get dressed and go out for a wander round the grounds".

register.evidence: A light, even Aussie layer, right for level 2: "bonzer", "mob", "righto", "reckoned"; no swearing.

tone.evidence: The dry, wry, second-person comedy is whole: "Some people _are_ like that."

flow.evidence: Smooth throughout: "Scratch the bath as too noisy. And so, very carefully, almost on the sly, you set about getting dressed."

problems.why: Slightly loses the grudging 'at that'; harmless.

C.summary: A light, natural, faithful retelling at the right weight; the best of the set with E.

meaning.evidence: Every point survives, close to the original's structure.

sense.evidence: Mostly exact ("have a squiz out", "scruffy-looking mob", "dodgy-looking barges"), but "perfectly ripper" strains: ripper doesn't take 'perfectly' easily.

authenticity.evidence: Mostly natural, with some stiff carry-overs: "You suppose they reckoned that'd be over your head, did they?", "Maybe open it modestly and have a squiz out".

register.evidence: A light layer at about level 2: "cos", "brekkie", "squiz", "uni", "righto".

tone.evidence: Keeps the wry deadpan: "Some people _are_ like that."

flow.evidence: Readable, with some clunky joins where slang meets the original's syntax: "Opening, at the red ribbon:" and "You suppose they reckoned".

problems.quote: The feeling behind this is perfectly ripper
problems.original: The sentiment in this attitude is perfectly bully

problems.quote: You suppose they reckoned that'd be over your head, did they?
problems.original: You suppose they thought that would be over your head, did they?
problems.why: 'You suppose they reckoned' stacks two verbs of thinking: clunky.

problems.quote: Maybe open it modestly and have a squiz out.
problems.original: Perhaps open it modestly and peer out.

D.summary: A faithful light retelling at the right weight; a little more literal and clunky than C or E.

meaning.evidence: Every point survives; "Takes you about two seconds" renders the work of a moment.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "no worries" for the simple problem, "have a squiz out", "Pretty scruffy-looking mob", "that vague it's downright terrifying". "It's a lovely thought, and all" loses a little of bully's slang flavour but keeps the sense.

authenticity.evidence: Natural throughout: "it's that vague it's downright terrifying", "Fair enough, I s'pose", "nothing for it but to get dressed".

register.evidence: A light-to-moderate layer, right for level 2: "no worries", "brekkie", "squiz", "mob", "'em".

tone.evidence: Keeps the wry, self-mocking deadpan: "Well, we'll show 'em! We'll read it just out of spite."

flow.evidence: Reads like it was written that way: "Back over onto the cool pillow till twenty past. Then up on your elbow again".

problems.quote: Hello, there's some books on the table.
problems.original: Hello, here are some books on the table.
problems.why: 'there's some books' is colloquial and fine aloud, but reads a touch sloppy on the page.
A slightly weaker rendering of the original's comic 'clandestinely'.

E.summary: A natural, varied, faithful light retelling; with C the best.
